# Introduction

**mechGEA** is a mechanistic genotype–environment association (GEA) pipeline
for identifying loci involved in local adaptation, designed to work directly
with low-coverage sequencing data.

This vignette walks through a complete analysis of the bundled example data set
(200 individuals in 20 patches, 1,500 loci, 5 environmental variables). The 
pipeline has three steps, which are *automatically run by the * `mechGEA()` 
*wrapper function*:

1. Preparing genotype likelihoods and patch metadata
2. Estimating migration between patches
3. Fit the GEA model
4. Summarize and plot results

## Why a mechanistic GEA?

Most GEA methods have two limitations:

1. **They ignore uncertainty in allele frequencies.** Allele frequencies are
   estimated from a finite, often incomplete sample of genotypes, and with
   low-coverage data the genotypes themselves are uncertain. Treating these
   estimates as known can bias downstream inference.
2. **They are phenomenological.** Regression-based approaches (e.g. GLMs)
   assume a particular shape for the relationship between environment and allele
   frequency, but are only loosely connected to evolutionary theory.

mechGEA instead builds the analysis on an explicit model of evolution.

## How it works

mechGEA is a hierarchical Bayesian model, with three linked levels:

- **Data model:** links the observed sequencing data to unobserved patch-level
  allele frequencies via genotype likelihoods, so uncertainty from low read
  depth, small samples and missing data is carried through the analysis.
- **Process model:** describes how evolutionary forces generate those allele
  frequencies. Building on Wright's island model, allele frequencies in each
  patch settle into an equilibrium shaped by drift, mutation and migration,
  tilted by selection whose strength depends on local environmental conditions.
  Each locus gets an environmental sensitivity coefficient (β); neutral loci
  have β ≈ 0, while adaptive loci track the environment across patches.
- **Parameter model:** encodes the expectation from neutral theory that most
  of the genome is not under local selection. A horseshoe prior on β shrinks
  most loci towards zero while letting a few strongly associated loci escape,
  which limits false positives across thousands of loci.

In practice, the pipeline (1) estimates migration among sampled patches,
(2) fits the GEA model while accounting for that migration, and (3) reports
per-locus, per-environment β estimates with credible intervals. Loci whose
credible intervals exclude zero are candidates for local adaptation.

# Installation

mechGEA fits its models with Stan (via `cmdstanr` and `rstan`) and handles
spatial data with `sf` and `terra`. Installing these dependencies manually can
be difficult, in part because they must be installed in a particular order under
different C++ compiler versions. The usual installation tools
(`install.packages` or the `remotes` and `pak` packages) cannot handle on their
own; installing with these tools alone will only produce a partial-install. We
therefore **strongly recommend installing mechGEA into a dedicated conda
environment** using a two-step process via the function `setup_mechGEA_env()`
included in mechGEA.

> mechGEA is currently tested and maintained for **Linux** only. Support for
> Windows and macOS is limited.

**1. Initial install of mechGEA** from GitHub, using `remotes` or `pak`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes") # skip if already installed!
remotes::install_github("hemstrow/mechGEA")
```

This will install the package, but the core functions will be turned off unless
a complete install is done. The full package install can then be completed with
the `setup_mechGEA_env()` utility.

**2. Build the complete environment** with `setup_mechGEA_env()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mechGEA::setup_mechGEA_env() # creates a conda environment called "mechGEA"
```

This builds a self-contained conda environment (using the `reticulate` package)
with everything mechGEA needs: R, C/C++/Fortran compilers, CmdStan, `cmdstanr`,
`rstan`, `sf`, `terra`, all other dependencies, and mechGEA itself. No system
libraries or administrator rights are required.
- If conda is not found, Miniconda is installed automatically. To use an
existing conda installation (other than the default), provide a path to the
conda executable: `setup_mechGEA_env(conda_path = "/path/to/conda")`.
- Use `name` to choose a different environment name. The function stops if an
environment with that name already exists.
- Setup compiles several packages and can take a long time. At the end, check
that the printed CmdStan path points inside the conda environment.

**3. Activate the environment** in bash to run analyses, then either run an R script or start up an R session:

```{bash, eval = FALSE}
conda activate mechGEA
Rscript path/to/my_analysis.R
```

`example_slurm_job()` (see *Large datasets*) depends on an installed
environment. For manual installation, try checking out the code executed by
`setup_mechGEA_env()` and following the install order noted there:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
example_slurm_job
```


# Check the installation

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(mechGEA)

# Run checks and return TRUE if everything is OK. Also run automatically, only
# needs to be run once per session.
check_correct_install() 

```


## Input data

mechGEA works from genotype likelihoods rather than called genotypes, so it
can be applied to any data from which likelihoods can be estimated, including
low-coverage whole-genome sequencing and reduced-representation (e.g. RADseq)
data. Likelihoods in BEAGLE format (e.g. from ANGSD) can be converted with
`beagle2pl()`.


# Quick-start Guide

Here, we will walk through a basic analysis of the example data included in
this package (`example_gl` and `sample_metadata`): 200 individuals
sampled across 20 patches, genotyped at 1,500 loci, with five environmental 
variables. We will look at the input formats, prepare patch metadata, 
estimate migration among patches, fit the mechanistic GEA model, and 
summarise and plot the results. We first run the full pipeline with 
a single call to `mechGEA()`, then step through each stage individually.

```{r}
library(mechGEA)
```

## Data import

mechGEA needs four inputs:

| Input | Description |
|---|---|
| `Phred` | Phred-scaled genotype likelihoods, one row per locus and one column per individual; genotypes comma separated with missing data marked "." |
| `patch_info` | Patch identification for each individual |
| `patches_xy` | Coordinates of each patch |
| `env` | Z-scaled (mean 0, sd 1), uncorrelated environmental variables for each patch |

For the example data, all four are stored in the `example_gl` list:

> **Important:** Individuals in `sample_metadata` must be in the **same order**
> as the columns (individuals) of the genotype likelihoods, and all individuals
> from the same patch must be in **consecutive rows**. Patches must in 
> `patches_xy` and `env` must also be sorted by order-of-appearance in 
> `patch_info`.


```{r}
str(example_gl, max.level = 1)
```

### Generating correctly formatted metadata from an `sf` object.

If your sample metadata is stored per individual in an `sf` object with one row
per individual and environmental values attached, as in the `sample_metadata`
example data, the`prepare_metadata()` function can be used to convert it into 
`patch_info`, `patches_xy`, and `env` objects:

```{r}
head(sample_metadata)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meta <- prepare_metadata(sample_metadata)
```

It is important to note that the GEA model assumes environmental variables are
uncorrelated and Z-scaled. The `prune_envs()` function can be used to prune
highly correlated environmental variables according to a correlation threshold
by sequentially removing the variables correlated with the highest number of
other variables. `prune_envs()` also Z-scales data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# removes one env from any pair with a correlation coefficient above 0.7
# (or below -0.7).
meta$env <- prune_envs(meta$env, r2 = 0.7)
```

The resulting, correctly formatted data should be essentially identical to that
in the `example_gl` data set, albeit without genotypes.

### Patch metadata details:

`patch_info` is a two-column data.frame with columns `ind_id` and `patch`.
Its rows must be in the same order as the columns of `Phred`, and 
**individuals must be sorted in blocks by patch**: all individuals 
from one patch must be in a block (sorted next to each other).

```{r}
head(example_gl$patch_info)
```

`patches_xy` gives coordinates for each patch, with columns `patch`, `lat` and
`lon`. `env` has a `patch` column followed by one column per environmental
variable, each Z-scaled (mean = 0, sd = 1). Lat/lon coordinates are recommended
to be in “WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)” coordinate reference for automatic plotting, but
this is not required. Both must list patches in the same order in which patches
first appear in `patch_info`.

```{r}
head(example_gl$patches_xy)
head(example_gl$env)
```

A quick sanity check before running anything:

```{r}
patch_order <- unique(example_gl$patch_info$patch)
identical(patch_order, example_gl$patches_xy$patch)
identical(patch_order, example_gl$env$patch)
identical(colnames(example_gl$likelihoods), example_gl$patch_info$ind_id)
```

All three should be `TRUE`. Note that these checks are also run automatically.

## Genotype likelihoods

Rather than called genotypes, mechGEA uses genotype likelihoods, so uncertainty
from low read depth is carried through the model. Each cell holds three 
comma-separated Phred-scaled likelihoods for the three possible genotypes 
(homozygous reference, heterozygote, homozygous alternate). Phred-scaling 
follows the equation:
\deqn{PL(\text{genotype}) = -10 \times \log_{10}\left( P(\text{Data} \mid \text{Genotype}) \right)}
with the lowest Phred-scaled genotype (the most likely genotype) assigned a zero
and everything else scaled to that value.


```{r}
dim(example_gl$likelihoods)          # loci x individuals
example_gl$likelihoods[1:5, 1:5]
```

Genotype likelihoods in BEAGLE format (for example, `.beagle.gz` output from
ANGSD) can be converted to this format with `beagle2pl()`. Each cell holds three
Phred-scaled genotype likelihoods (AA, AB, BB), (again, rescaled so the most
likely genotype is 0). Correspondingly, a phred-likelihood of 10 means that
genotype is 10× less likely than the likelihood with a score of 0. "." marks
missing data.

An example BEAGLE file is included with the package:

```{r}
bfile <- system.file("extdata", "example.beagle.gz", package = "mechGEA")
Phred <- beagle2pl(bfile)
dim(Phred)
```

`beagle2pl()` does not keep sample names from the beagle file by default (since
many programs, like ANGSD, name individuals "Ind0" through "Ind(n-1)"). The
`beagle2pl()` function allows for sample names to be provided via the 
`ind_names` argument.

**Note: this assumes `sample_metadata` is in the same order as the BAM list used 
to create the BEAGLE file.** If it is not, provide `ind_names` in the BAM list
order and use the `ind_order` argument to resort individuals on read-in. This
can also be used to re-sort individuals which are not in blocks by patch.

```{r}
colnames(Phred) <- sample_metadata$ind_id
Phred[1:5, 1:5]
```

# Running the full pipeline

`mechGEA()` runs every step of the analysis in one call:

1. **Data preparation**: validates the inputs, converts Phred scores to
   log-likelihoods, and builds the data for both models.
2. **Migration estimation**: fits the Bayesian migration model on a random
   subset of loci.
3. **GEA model fitting**: fits the mechanistic GEA model to all loci,
   accounting for the estimated migration.
4. **Summaries and plots**: identifies adaptive (locus, environment) pairs and
   plots the results.
5. **Effective sample size**: estimates effective sample sizes for each locus/
   environmental variable pair.

Results are returned as a list and also written to `files/` and `plot/` in the
**current working directory**, so run it in a dedicated folder.

The settings below are deliberately small so that the example finishes
quickly (about an hour on a 22-core server). They are **not** suitable for real
analyses; use the defaults, or larger values, for those.


```{r, eval = FALSE}

res <- mechGEA(Phred      = example_gl$likelihoods,
               patch_info = example_gl$patch_info,
               patches_xy = example_gl$patches_xy,
               env        = example_gl$env,
               migration_loci    = 1000,   # loci used to estimate migration
               N_sim_mig         = 20,
               chains_mig        = 2,
               iter_warmup_mig   = 200,
               iter_sampling_mig = 200,
               iter_warmup_gea   = 100,
               iter_sampling_gea = 100,
               par = 12)                   # cores to use
str(res, max.level = 1)

```

Each step in the pipeline has quite a few arguments; these are described in `mechGEA`'s documentation.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?mechGEA
```

# Step by step

The same analysis can be run one stage at a time, which is useful for checking model fits along the way or reusing intermediate results.

## 1. Prepare data

`prepare_mig_data()` builds the input data for both the migration model and the GEA model:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
dat <- prepare_mig_data(Phred      = example_gl$likelihoods,
                        patch_info = example_gl$patch_info,
                        patches_xy = example_gl$patches_xy,
                        env        = example_gl$env,
                        migration_loci = 200,
                        N_sim_mig      = 20)
names(dat)
```

## 3. Check effective sample size

Before fitting any models, it is worth checking how much information your
data actually contain. With low-coverage data, each sequenced individual
carries less information than a confidently genotyped one. `estimate_neff()`
estimates the effective number of individuals given the observed genotype
uncertainty, reported as N_eff / N (1 = no information lost to low coverage).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
neff <- estimate_neff(dat$stan_data)
str(neff, max.level = 1)
```

| Element | Contents |
|---|---|
| `loci_used` | Loci used for the estimate (a random subset of up to 1,000) |
| `TwoN_eff_*` | Effective number of allele copies sampled, per locus (rows) and patch (columns) |
| `G_eff_*` | Effective allele counts, per locus and patch |
| `*_stan` / `*_ana` | Estimates from the Stan model and from an analytical approximation |
| `Neff_mean` | Mean ratio of effective to actual sample size (1 = no information lost) |

In the example data, mean N_eff / N was about 0.80, so 200 low-coverage
individuals carry roughly the information of 160 high-coverage individuals.
This step takes a few minutes (~4-6 min for the example data).

## 3. Estimate migration

`estimate_migration()` fits the Bayesian migration model. 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mig <- estimate_migration(dat$migration_data,
                          chains_mig = 2,
                          iter_warmup_mig = 200,
                          iter_sampling_mig = 200,
                          par = 4)

plot_migration(mig, dat$migration_data, example_gl$patches_xy)
```

## 4. Fit the GEA model

`run_stan_GEA_model()` fits the mechanistic GEA model, accounting for estimated migration:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gea <- run_stan_GEA_model(dat$stan_data, mig,
                          iter_warmup_gea = 100,
                          iter_sampling_gea = 100,
                          par = 4)
names(gea)
```

## 5. Summarise and plot

Each locus gets an environmental sensitivity coefficient (β) for each environmental variable. `beta_summary()` summarizes their posterior distributions, and `plot_gea()` plots them. Loci whose credible intervals exclude zero are candidates for local adaptation. The `beta_summary` step is the most memory-intensive step of the entire pipeline. For high-performance computing (HPC) clusters, it might be a good idea to set-up a pipeline manually and allow more memory for this step if needed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
env_names <- colnames(example_gl$env)[-1]

bs <- beta_summary(gea$beta_draw,
                   nloci = nrow(example_gl$likelihoods),
                   nenv  = length(env_names))
head(bs$beta_summary)

plot_gea(dat$stan_data, mig, gea$beta_draw, bs$beta_summary,
         gea$rho_kappa_mu, env_names = env_names, CI = 0.95)
```

# Outputs

`mechGEA()` returns a list with seven elements:

| Element | Contents |
|---|---|
| `SNP_pvalues` | Association results for every (locus, environment) pair |
| `GEA_results` | Posterior draws and summaries from the GEA model |
| `migration_results` | Estimated patch × patch migration matrix |
| `Neff_results` | Effective sample size estimates (see *Check effective sample size*) |
| `migration_plot` | Migration plots (ggplot objects) |
| `GEA_plots` | GEA plots (ggplot objects) |
| `stan_and_migration_data` | The prepared model inputs (`stan_data` and `migration_data`) |

## Association results

`SNP_pvalues` is a data.table with one row per (locus, environment) pair
(1,500 loci × 5 environments = 7,500 rows):

| Column | Contents |
|---|---|
| `SNP` | Locus index (row of `Phred`) |
| `Env` | Environmental variable |
| `nlogp` | −log(p) for the association; larger values mean stronger evidence |

A pair is called adaptive when `nlogp` exceeds −log(1 − 0.95), which is about 3.0.
This is the horizontal line in the Manhattan plot.
To list the adaptive pairs:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
adaptive <- res$SNP_pvalues[nlogp > -log(1 - 0.95)]
nrow(adaptive)    # 23 in the example data
head(adaptive)
```

## GEA model results

`beta_summary` gives one row per β, named `Beta[e, l]` for environment `e` and
locus `l` (e.g. `Beta[3,1]` is locus 1's sensitivity to `env3`):

| Column | Contents |
|---|---|
| `variable` | Parameter name, `Beta[environment, locus]` |
| `mean`, `median` | Posterior mean and median of β |
| `sd`, `mad` | Posterior standard deviation and median absolute deviation |
| `q5`, `q95` | 5% and 95% posterior quantiles  |
| `rhat` | R-hat convergence diagnostic (should be close to 1) |
| `ess_bulk`, `ess_tail` | Effective sample sizes of the posterior draws |

Note that `q5`/`q95` are fixed at a 90% interval.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
head(res$GEA_results$beta_summary)
```

## Migration matrix

`migration_results` is a symmetric patch × patch matrix of **posterior mean**
migration rates. Off-diagonal entries are the migration rates between pairs of
patches (relative rates, for the default `migration_fast` model). This
matrix can be passed to later runs through `migration_results` (see *Large
datasets*); as in the GEA model, the posterior mean is treated as known.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
round(res$migration_results[1:5, 1:5], 2)
head(res$migration_results)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
str(res, max.level = 1)
head(res$SNP_pvalues)
```

It also writes intermediate results and plots to the working directory:

- `files/`: `.RDS` files from each stage (`1_` data preparation, `2_` migration,
  `4_` GEA model, `5_` adaptive loci, `6_` effective sample size). These can be
  reloaded with `readRDS()` without re-running the model.
- `plot/`: PDF figures, shown below.

Because migration results are saved, they can be reused for other runs via
`migration_results = res$migration_results` (see *Large datasets*). Plots of 
migration results are also stored in `$migration_plot`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res$migration_plot$IBD # plot of isolation-by-distance
res$migration_plot$map # plot of connectivity on space
```


## Genotype–environment associations

The GEA results generate three plots (alongside the p-values discussed above):

### Manhattan plots

The Manhattan plot shows the evidence for association at each locus for each
environmental variable. In the example data, mechGEA identifies **~23 adaptive
(locus, environment) pairs** at a 95% credible interval. Manhattan plots are
stored at.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res$GEA_plots$manhattan
```

Note that the `plot_manhattan` function cann be used if multiple runs were conducted
or if more detailed chromosomal locations are available for each locus. The first
argument takes either a `mechGEA` result, the `$SNP_pvalues` table of a `mechGEA`
result, or a list containing multiple of either (mixing OK). The second argument
takes either a table of locus metadata (columns "SNP", "CHROM", and "POS"),
a path to the beagle file which was used to run the data, or a list containing
multiple of either.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
beagle <- system.file("extdata", "example.beagle.gz", package = "mechGEA")
plot_manhattan(res, beagle)
```

### Migration-selection balance plots

[NIKUNJ PLEASE CHECK THIS]

The balance between migration and selection at each adaptive locus. Each panel
shows one adaptive locus, with patches plotted against the associated
environmental variable. Blue points ("No migration") are the expected allele
frequency in each patch under local selection alone, treating patches as
isolated. Orange points ("Mean-field (1st correction)") add migration: each
patch's expected frequency is shifted toward the frequency of its immigrants,
i.e. the migration-weighted average of the other patches' no-migration
frequencies. Values are averaged over posterior draws, and arrows run from the
no-migration to the migration-corrected value.

Short arrows mean selection dominates and the patch stays near its locally
favoured frequency. Long arrows mean gene flow pulls the patch away from its
local optimum, which is strongest for patches that receive many migrants from
patches with different favoured frequencies.

For each adaptive (locus, environment) pair, selection in each patch is
s = β × (environmental value of that patch), so patches with more extreme
environments experience stronger selection, and the sign of β sets its
direction. ρ, by contrast, scales how strongly migration affects that locus.
In the migration–selection balance plot, only the associated environmental
variable is used for each locus.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res$GEA_plots$migration_selection_balance
```

### Association plots
Association plots show the strength and direction of genotype-environment association for each significantly asosciated locus/environment pair.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res$GEA_plots$association_plots
```


# Large datasets

Whole-genome data sets are usually too large to fit in a single model run. The
recommended approach is to split the data into chunks of loci and run each
chunk separately, ideally in parallel on a computing cluster.

mechGEA has a few utilities to help with this:

1. `get_chunks()` splits a ".beagle" or ".beagle.gz" file into chunks containing n loci.
2. `example_slurm_job` generates directories, data and metadata files, and a ready-to-run job script for SLURM clusters (which can be modified for other job-management engines). This script will run `mechGEA` on each BEAGLE chunk.

## Splitting data into chunks 

`get_chunks()` splits a BEAGLE file into smaller BEAGLE files of
`loci_per_chunk` loci each, reading the input in pieces so that the full file
never has to be loaded into memory. e.g recommended 50k SNPs per chunk at max
for whole genome dataset

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bfile  <- system.file("extdata", "example.beagle.gz", package = "mechGEA")
chunks <- get_chunks(bfile, 
                     loci_per_chunk = 500, # loci per chunk, use 50-100k for WGS
                     outdir = ".") # save files to pwd. Default uses beagle dir.
chunks
#> [1] "chunk_0.beagle.gz" "chunk_1.beagle.gz" "chunk_2.beagle.gz"
```

## Running on a SLURM cluster

`example_slurm_job()` generates a SLURM array job that runs `mechGEA()` on each
BEAGLE file as a separate task:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sh <- example_slurm_job(beagle_files    = chunks,
                        sample_metadata = sample_metadata,
                        output_dir      = "results",
                        conda_env       = "mechGEA")
sh
```

Note that the `example_slurm_job` can take all of the arguments to `mechGEA` and
will also prune environmental variables using `prune_envs()` according to the
supplied arguments. `example_slurm_job` also takes a handful of resource 
arguments and can automatically install a conda environment. See the 
documentation for details:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?example_slurm_job
```


This writes the following files to `./control/` (change this with
`control_file_prefix`):

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `example_slurm_array_job.sh` | SLURM array script, one task per BEAGLE file |
| `example_array_rscript.R` | R script run by each task |
| `beaglelist.txt` | list of BEAGLE files |
| `sample_metadata.RDS` | prepared metadata (`patch_info`, `patches_xy`, `env`) |
| `parmfile.RDS` | additional arguments passed to `mechGEA()` |

Each task converts its BEAGLE file with `beagle2pl()`, runs `mechGEA()` in its
own sub-directory of `output_dir` (`partition_<task>_<chunk name>`), and
writes its results there. The final outputs (e.g. the results of `res <- mechGEA(...)`) will be saved
as `final_results.RDS`.

## Manhattan plots across many results

## Reusing migration estimates

Migration only needs to be estimated once. Using one chunk to estimate migration
may be desirable to reduce runtime. To do so, estimate migration from a subset
of loci with `stop_after_migration = TRUE`, then pass the result to every task
through `migration_results`, so that all chunks share the same migration
estimate:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# first, run on one chunk--set these to read in and run on your mig chunk
mig_phred <- beagle2pl("path/to/my/chunk.beagle.gz")
mig_run <- mechGEA(Phred      = mig_phred,
                   patch_info = example_gl$patch_info,
                   patches_xy = example_gl$patches_xy,
                   env        = example_gl$env,
                   stop_after_migration = TRUE)

# save the migration results:
saveRDS(mig_run$migration_results, "mig_res.RDS")

sh <- example_slurm_job(beagle_files      = chunks,
                        sample_metadata   = example_gl,
                        output_dir        = "results",
                        conda_env         = "mechGEA",
                        migration_results = "mig_res.RDS")
```

## Before submitting

The generated shell script is a template and **must be edited to match your
cluster** before use (see the notes at the top of the file). 

```{bash, eval = FALSE}
sbatch control/example_slurm_array_job.sh
```

## Combining manhattan plots

As mentioned above, the `plot_manhattan` function can be used to combine plot results across runs.

```{r, eval = FALSE}

results <- c("path/to/partion_1/final_results.RDS",
             ..., # list the rest of the files
             "path/to/partion_n/final_results.RDS")

chunks <- c("path/to/partion_1/input.beagle.gz",
             ..., # list the rest of the files
             "path/to/partion_n/input.beagle.gz")

plot_manhattan(results, chunks)

```

If you use mechGEA, please also cite:

> Goel, N., Bossu, C.M., Van Ee, J.J., Zavaleta, E., Ruegg, K.C. & Hooten, M.B.
> (2025). Identifying genomic adaptation to local climate using a mechanistic
> evolutionary model. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 16(10), 2448–2460.
> <https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.70117>

> Goel, N., Bossu, C.M., Yi, S., Robertson, E.C., Brown, T.M., Bolton, P.E.,
> Vernasco, B.J., Amirkhiz, R.G., Zavaleta, E., Ruegg, K.C. & Hooten, M.B. 
> (2026). Identifying adaptive variation in spatially structured populations 
> using low-coverage whole-genome sequencing data. 
> *Molecular Biology and Evolution*, 43(10), msag255. 
> <https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msag255>

## Runtime

On a 12-core server, the example above (1,500 loci, 200 individuals, with the
quick settings) took about one hour:

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| Data preparation | ~15 s |
| Migration model | ~1.5 min |
| GEA model | ~52 min |
| Plotting | ~1 min |
| Effective sample size | ~6 min |

The GEA model dominates runtime and scales with the number of loci and
iterations, so for genome-scale data use the chunked workflow described below.
